Cape Train Drama

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Every morning, at 6.30 on radio cape talk 567 a person comes on mic and details the number of train cancellations or delays, and on one day I counted about 25 such trains. It plays havoc with poor commuters who often find themselves then getting to work late and losing their jobs.

There are a number of reasons: poor maintenance on the lines, theft of copper cables, violence on the trains and then some of them have been burnt already by angry commuters or security gaurs.New trains are only expected in about 3 years time. But as you know, the life line of any economy is an effect transport system. And it Cape Town this is being felt.

This insert looks into the issues facing metro rail in cape town and its impact on workers who often now have to get jup at 4 am in order to make sure that they get to work in time.

The issues are: criminal action (once we had the railway police which would travel on tains, this does not happen any more). We speak to one man who heroically saved the lives of commuters and who himself was thrown off the train. We look at the cable theft and also hear that a new law is being promulgated which will send offenders of cable theft to prison for a mononum of 5 years. We will look at the fight between the secutity company which tried to look after the safety of commuters and which were made redundant.

But we will also look at the economy and why some people are being fired. Large companies can absorb people coming late, it’s the small SMO’s that suffer the most. Michael Bagraim, attorney, conducted research on the dilemma – and he got 650 responses from 3000 questionnaires that he sent out. It showed that the most vulnerable to the effects of train delays were the small smo’s , the life blood of economy. If a capetner came late, and affected then a crew of 5, then work would be lost for the whole day.


Further information:
The story will be told through an activist group called, the Cape Train voice, the attorney Michael Baigmram, a commuter who was fired, a commuter who gets up at 4 am – and victims of violence, and the hero who stopped an attack.

Press Release:


Cape Metrorail
For several months the Cape Metrorail system has been in crisis. Old trains, vandalism and under-investment in infrastructure have resulted in daily cancellations and numerous delays. The city’s unreliable trains have wreaked havoc with the lives of desperate commuters, some of whom have lost their jobs after repeatedly arriving late for work. Carte Blanche asks: what does the future hold for Cape Town’s passenger rail network?


Script:


A taxi pulls up outside a popular coffee shop in Green Point, Cape Town and offloads barista Soul Chalemba. Normally he would travel in from the Cape Flats by train but he has to be at work on time to help set up the shop and serve customers.

Saul: I have to come by taxi because the trains they always making some delays.

Radio Sound Up: Our normal woes continue on the northern line every single morning, we've got 12 trains cancelled.

And those delays feature ever morning on the traffic reports at Cape Town radio station Cape Talk.

Acts of sabotage and arson have taken their toll. According to Cape Metrorail from October 2015 to April 2016 they were losing a passenger capacity of around 40 000 everyday. With 34 trains being cancelled daily. Sometimes resulting in massive overcrowding.

We went to see for ourselves. The train we were due to catch was cancelled so we waited for the next one.

LINK: Well it’s just after 7:15. We are the train station in Mandalay, Khayelitsha. We are about to board a train to Cape Town and this one is only a few minutes late.

We boarded a third class coach to experience what commuters are dealing with everyday. We were met by a preacher’s passionate voice, which was followed by impromptu singing.

LINK: Well here we are in third class and in the background songs of worship, which is probably appropriate given that very often you may get to work on a wing and prayer.

At times frustrated passengers become stranded between stations when their trains grind to a halt, making them late for work and putting their jobs in jeopardy.

Bargain: And so the issue is people are getting dismissed and they getting dismissed on a daily basis.

Labor lawyer Michael Bargain is an independent arbiter who chairs disciplinary enquiries. He often has the unenviable task of dismissing employees on behalf of his clients.

Bargain: So I must have by now dismissed 30 people of the last 6 months for late coming because of the trains which means that these people will probably never find a job again. It’s a horrific story.

LINK: We appear to have reached a point where train delays particularly in Cape Town have become almost endemic and the question is what exactly is the cause?

That question we posed to Richard Walker who heads up Cape Metrorail and who also uses the train to get to and from work.

John: You are dealing with a serious headache. This is a major problem for you?
Richard Walker: Definitely John. We have been given a set back with the incidents of deliberate arson to our train sets since October last year.

The train crisis reached a peak in April this year when several trains were set alight at Cape Town station. As well as a huge signal apparatus at Salt River junction, which almost brought the city to a standstill. Over an 8-month period 52 coaches were burned and in the same period there were hundreds of acts of vandalism and theft on Signal Equipment.

Walker: We not alone in this situation if you look at what’s happening across the country, even the city, you know where state assets unfortunately has become sort of fair game for any sort of cause.

Passengers are also fair game for criminals. In April this year Capetonian Darryn August went to the aid of fellow passengers who were being robbed by a gang. He was stabbed and struck on the head.

Darryn August: I was seeing double. I couldn’t really see properly what was in front of me and one of the guys just decided to just throw me out.

Darryn was flung from a moving train and fractured his spine. He's been hailed as a hero but it is feared he will never be able to walk again.

Darryn August: I don’t think I'll do anything differently so I don’t think I'm a hero I just think I'm a normal guy that just wants to the right thing.

Budget constraints mean that Metrorail cant provide security on all trains. Last year thought they claimed that 1702 arrests were made for train related offences and if a serious crime is committed on a train or a person is struck by a passing train, it has to stop for a police investigation. Criminality combined with aging rolling stock and infrastructures are presenting Cape Metrorail with severe challenges, which then inevitably impact employers. Recently the Cape Chamber of Commerce conducted research amongst its members into the effect of train delays.

John: What are your members saying? They must be pulling their hair out?
Janine Myburgh: Very much so on a daily basis. I mean it affects productivity. IT increases absenteeism. It lowers morale. People don’t know whether they are going to get to work. Employers don’t know whether their employees are going to come to the work and the bottom line doesn’t change, the work still has to be done.

85% of employers said that train delays had a demotivating effect on employees.
47% said they had introduced flexi time and 84% said that productivity had been affected.

Janine Myburgh: So it goes without saying for the economy to function optimally, we need a functioning rail system.

The research also found that 39% of employers were considering penalties for latecomers.

Bargain: We have almost 90% of our work force catch the trains which is fantastic, tis a great story because it eases on the congestion on the roads, it eases the problem with petrol and road usage and all sorts of other things and yet we not delivering. We not getting the people to work.

Worst affected are small businesses because the late arrival of one employee can have a knock on effect.
Jordi Kushner: So if he is late there is a chain effect for the whole day cause we have cars that are being sold that are going out and we got to prep them and know exactly where we going and if he is an hour or two late it delays the whole team.

Employee Michael Malate needs to arrive early to open up the business. Often he is late and he is fed up.

Michael Malate: I don't feel happy. I don’t feel right because I must talk with work and I must have excuses at work.
John: You say that things are getting worse?
Jordi: It is definitely getting worse. I would say it used to be maybe once or twice a month. It's probably once a week now.

Malate’s job though is safe because owner Jordi Kushner understands his predicament.

LINK: A local innovator has come to the rescue of frustrated Cape Town commuters. He ahs developed an app, which amongst other things lets their bosses know when they will be late for work.

This app, which covers all of South Africa, provides timetables as well as up to date delays and cancellations.

Domenico Deidda: So an employee would be on the train. They would be delayed and they would need to communicate to their boss or inform them in a sense in an official way that they are going to be late and they go to the app, fill out their details, fill out their bosses email address and would send the boss an email informing them that the employee would be late for a specific reason.


The good news is that there is some light at the end of the tunnel.

Walker: There has been a very deliberate decision and strategy implemented by national government by the department of transport which is enabling PRASA to modernize the passenger rail system in the country.

PRASA is committed to spending 172 billion rand over the next ten years for passenger rail but new trains are only expected in Cape Town in about 2019. However cape Metrorail says it has an incidence and recovery plan in place to repair and refurbish damaged trains and keep the existing ones operational. In the meantime Soul Chalemba is having to spend a significant portion of his salary on ensuring he arrives at work on time.

Soul: The train is cheap because I can spend only R150 a month for the train where the taxi, I'm spending R1200 a month.

Its for this reason and the fact that workers pay packets are being docked because of late arrivals that Cosatu is planning a major strike in Cape Town to express is dissatisfaction at the current rail service.
